# Prompting and In-Context Learning {#sec-prompting}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements here were run on the same
Turkish product-review corpus as @sec-bake-off and @sec-classification —
233,508 de-duplicated reviews — but on a **balanced** sample rather than the
natural 93.7%-positive distribution, so that accuracy is readable against a
50% floor and the effect being measured is the prompt rather than the class
prior. Every prompt variant measured here is **zero-shot**: the in-context
learning half of the title is carried by the literature and by
@sec-classification's few-shot numbers rather than by a measurement of its own.
The $k$-shot curve this chapter ought to have — accuracy against number of
demonstrations, run twice with gold and with random labels — is
@sec-prompting-exercises' third exercise, and it is the measurement we would add
first. Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `qwen3.5:9b`, Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain what in-context learning is and why putting examples in a prompt
  changes behaviour without changing a single weight;
- apply the pattern library — role, structure, demonstrations, decomposition —
  and say what each one is actually for;
- write a prompt as a *specification* with an output contract, rather than as
  a request;
- measure how much of your score is the prompt rather than the model, and
  build the evaluation that makes prompt changes reviewable.

## Why prompting works at all {#sec-prompting-why}

A pretrained model predicts the next token. Nothing in that objective says it
should follow an instruction, and the first large models mostly did not — you
had to trick them, by writing a prefix whose natural continuation happened to
be the answer you wanted.

@reynolds2021prompt is the historical document for that era, and reading it
now is a good reminder of how much of "prompt engineering" was working around
a missing capability.

Two things changed. **Scale** made models able to infer a task from examples
in the context [@brown2020language], and **instruction tuning**, followed by
preference training (@sec-post-training), trained them to treat an instruction
as an instruction rather than as text to continue. The second is why modern prompting feels like
asking rather than tricking.

::: {#gloss-in-context-learning .column-margin .term-gloss}
**in-context learning** (bağlam içi öğrenme) — the model doing better at a
task because examples of it are sitting in the prompt. No weight is updated
and nothing survives the call, which is why *learning* is a slightly
misleading word for it.
[↩](#term-in-context-learning){.term-back}
:::

[In-context learning](#gloss-in-context-learning){#term-in-context-learning .term-ref}
is the first of those: you put input-output pairs in the prompt, and the model
does better on the next input, **with no parameter updated and nothing retained
after the call**.

Two words you will meet constantly name how many examples you give. A
**zero-shot** prompt has none — only the instruction and the input. A
**few-shot** prompt adds a handful of *demonstrations* (input–output pairs), and
*$k$-shot* names the exact number: an 8-shot prompt carries eight.

So it is not learning in the sense @sec-post-training uses the word — nothing is
fitted, nothing persists. That is a claim about the *mechanism*, not about what
the model can pick up: a mapping it genuinely acquires from the context is still
acquired from the context, and a paragraph below names exactly that case. A
useful working description of the common case is *task inference*: the examples
narrow down which task you are asking for, out of the many the model already
knows how to do.

That framing predicts something odd, and the prediction holds.
@min2022rethinking replaced the labels in the demonstrations with **random**
ones and found performance mostly survived. What the examples were mainly
conveying was the *shape* of the task — the label space, the format, the
distribution of inputs — not the input-to-label mapping.

That is worth knowing before you spend a week curating perfect examples.

Two lines of work say *how* that narrowing happens, and they are worth having
because "task inference" is otherwise just a phrase. @xie2022explanation
formalises it as implicit Bayesian inference: the demonstrations sharpen a
posterior over latent concepts the model already acquired in pretraining, which
is why the *distribution* of the examples matters more than their correctness.
@olsson2022induction gives the circuit-level version — attention heads that
complete `[A][B] … [A] → [B]`, which appear at exactly the point in training
where in-context learning ability jumps. After @sec-transformers, that is the
hardware answer to "how can examples in a prompt work without changing a
weight".

And a limit on @min2022rethinking worth carrying, because this chapter repeats
it several times. @pan2023incontext separates **task recognition** — the
demonstrations tell the model *which* task — from **task learning**, where they
teach it the mapping. Random labels leave task recognition intact, which is what
Min et al. measured; task learning does exist, grows with model scale, and is
exactly what random labels destroy. So "the labels do not matter" is true of the
recognition part and false of the learning part, and it is not a licence to use
wrong labels.

::: {.column-margin}
It also predicts the failure mode. If demonstrations mostly convey format,
then a model that already knows the format gains little from them — which is
exactly what @sec-classification measured, where eight examples were worth
+7.17 macro-F1 on one model and +0.51 ($p = 0.62$) on a stronger one. The
technique did not stop working; the models stopped needing it.
:::

### The claim this chapter is built on

[The prompt is part of the model.]{.hl} Not a message to it — a component of
the system, sitting in the same position a feature-extraction function sits in
@sec-bake-off's pipeline. It has a version, it has a contract, it has
regressions, and changing it changes your output distribution as surely as
swapping the checkpoint would.

The rest of the chapter is what follows from taking that seriously, and
@sec-prompting-brittle is the measurement that makes it hard to avoid.

**What we will look at.** First the pattern library — five things that work,
and what job each one is actually doing, so you can tell when a pattern will
not help. Then the shift from writing requests to writing specifications,
which is what makes a prompt checkable at all. Then the measurement this
chapter turns on: twelve prompts that mean the same thing, spanning almost
fifteen points of accuracy on one model and one task, with the role prefix
finishing eleventh of twelve. And finally the machinery that follows once you
accept the number — reproducibility, a frozen set, paired tests, and a version
string.

## A pattern library {#sec-prompting-patterns}

If the prompt is a component, these are its parts. Five patterns cover most of
what works, and none of them is a magic word — each is doing an identifiable
job, and naming the job is what tells you when the pattern will not help.

**Role.** *You are an experienced customer-feedback analyst.* The job is to
select a region of the model's distribution — vocabulary, register, what
counts as a relevant detail. It is weakest when it asks for expertise the
model does not have (a role prefix does not make a model a doctor) and
strongest when it disambiguates *style*, which is a real and frequent need.

In a chat model, the role and any standing rules usually go in the **system
prompt** — a separate message, before the user's turn, that the chat template
(@sec-post-training) marks with its own tokens. Models are trained to give it
priority over what the user writes, but it is still text in the same context
window, not a setting the model cannot ignore: it makes instructions *stronger*,
not *tamper-proof*.

**Structure.** Sections, delimiters, an explicit place for the input. The job
is to make the boundary between your instruction and the user's data
unambiguous. `<review>...</review>` is not decoration; it is what tells the
model which span is data. Be precise about what it is not: a delimiter *marks*
that boundary, it does not *enforce* it. Text inside the tags is still text the
model reads, and a review that closes the tag and issues its own instruction is
the standard attack, *prompt injection* — @sec-agent-security is where that is treated as the
security problem it is, and structure alone is not a defence.

**Demonstrations.** Input-output pairs. The job, per @min2022rethinking, is
mainly to fix the *format and label space*. Use them when the output shape is
unusual or hard to describe, and expect less from them when the task is one
the model has obviously seen.

**Decomposition.** Ask for one thing at a time, or ask for intermediate
results before the answer. The job is to move work out of a single forward
pass and into tokens — which is @sec-reasoning's subject, and where the
measurement of when it helps lives. This chapter's contribution is the
practical corollary: **a prompt that asks for four things at once will do at
least one of them badly**, and splitting it is usually cheaper than fixing it.

**Output contract.** State the exact shape of the answer, and make it the
easiest thing for the model to produce. This is the pattern with the most
leverage and it gets its own section.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What about "think step by step"?

This is the prompted form of *chain-of-thought*: the model writes intermediate
steps before its final answer. It belongs to @sec-reasoning, which measures it
properly, and the short answer is that the phrase is largely a relic.
@kojima2022large found it worked on models that had not been trained to reason; models that *have* been trained to reason
produce the trace whether or not you ask, and adding the phrase to a reasoning
model mostly wastes tokens.

The durable part is not the phrase but the mechanism: more tokens before the
answer means more computation available to produce it. Ask for intermediate
results when the task needs them, and skip the incantation.
:::

## Prompts as specifications {#sec-prompting-spec}

The most useful shift in this chapter is grammatical: stop writing prompts as
*requests* and start writing them as *specifications*.

A request says what you want. A specification says what a valid output is —
which means it can be checked, and a prompt whose output can be checked is a
prompt you can test.

```text
request         "Summarise the customer's complaint."

specification   "Return one JSON object with keys `issue` (string, max 15
                 words), `severity` (one of: low, medium, high) and
                 `product` (string, copied exactly from the review, or null
                 if no product is named). Return nothing else."
```

The second version gives you three things the first does not: a parser that
either succeeds or fails loudly, a set of values you can validate, and a
`null` that gives the model a legal way to say *no product is named* instead of
inventing one — though, as @sec-decoding stresses, you still have to check that
the model actually uses it.

Three rules that follow:

1. **Name the failure output.** If the model cannot comply, what should it
   return? A prompt without an escape hatch gets a fabricated answer instead
   of an admission, because you left the model no legal way to say no.
2. **Put the constraint where it binds.** An instruction 800 tokens above the
   input competes with the input for attention. Constraints that must hold go
   close to the end.
3. **Make the contract machine-checkable, then check it.** A schema you do not
   validate is a comment. @sec-decoding is where the enforcement machinery
   lives — grammars, JSON Schema, and the measurement of what constraining
   costs.

::: {.column-margin}
And a warning from @sec-sequence-labeling-llm, which is worth repeating in the chapter
where the schema gets written rather than the one where it gets enforced: a
schema guarantees *shape*, never *truth*. A grammar-constrained call happily
returned `{"answer": 1}` for the capital of France. Validating the contract
tells you the output is well-formed and nothing else.
:::

## How much of your score is the prompt? {#sec-prompting-brittle}

Everything above is craft. This section is the measurement that makes the
craft matter, and it is the one to run on your own task before you trust any
number you have.

Twelve prompts were written for the same task — decide whether a Turkish
product review is positive or negative. **A competent reader would call them
the same instruction.**

They differ in formatting, in the surface form of the labels, in where the
review sits relative to the instruction, in delimiters, and in politeness. None
changes the task or the criteria.

Three of them do change what the labels *are*, and that turns out to be
informative rather than a flaw in the design: `A`/`B` and `1`/`0` strip the
labels of meaning entirely, and `olumlu`/`olumsuz` changes their language. Hold
that in mind for the table — the semantically empty `A`/`B` finishes **second**,
ahead of the meaningful Turkish pair by more than ten points. The model is not
reading the labels as words. It is reading them as slots.

| variant | what it changes against `baseline` |
|:--|:--|
| `baseline` | — instruction, then the review, then `Answer:`; labels `positive` / `negative` |
| `label positive/negative` | label surface form |
| `label A/B` | label surface form, meaning removed |
| `label 1/0` | label surface form, meaning removed |
| `label olumlu/olumsuz` | label surface form, language changed to Turkish |
| `bulleted` | the instruction laid out as bullets |
| `numbered` | the instruction laid out as numbered lines |
| `triple quotes` | the review wrapped in `"""…"""` |
| `xml delimiters` | the review wrapped in `<review>…</review>` |
| `review first` | the review moved above the instruction |
| `polite` | a *lütfen* prefix and a *teşekkürler* suffix |
| `role prefix` | a one-sentence persona prepended |

: What each variant changes {tbl-colwidths="[34,66]"}

One thing this chapter owes you and does not supply: the full text of all
twelve. The table above names what changes; it does not let you reproduce the
run, and a prompt experiment whose prompts are not printed is not reproducible.
Print yours.

All twelve ran on the same 150 balanced reviews, same model, temperature 0,
fixed seed. Every response parsed; nothing was dropped. The intervals below are
*Wilson* intervals — a 95% confidence interval for a proportion that, unlike the
textbook $\hat p \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}$, stays sensible near 0% and 100%.

```text
variant                        acc      95% CI (Wilson)
label positive/negative     90.00%   [ 84.2,  93.8]
label A/B                   88.67%   [ 82.6,  92.8]
bulleted                    87.33%   [ 81.1,  91.7]
numbered                    87.33%   [ 81.1,  91.7]
label 1/0                   86.67%   [ 80.3,  91.2]
triple quotes               82.00%   [ 75.1,  87.3]
baseline                    79.33%   [ 72.2,  85.0]
label olumlu/olumsuz        78.00%   [ 70.7,  83.9]
xml delimiters              77.33%   [ 70.0,  83.3]
polite                      76.67%   [ 69.3,  82.7]
role prefix                 76.00%   [ 68.6,  82.1]
review first                75.33%   [ 67.9,  81.5]

spread 75.33% – 90.00% = 14.67 points     mean 82.06   sd 5.57
```

**A range needs something to be a range against.** If all twelve prompts were
equally good and each score were an independent draw at $n = 150$, the standard
error on one estimate would be 3.13 points and the *expected* spread of twelve
such draws about **10 points** — from sampling noise alone. So 14.67 is roughly
one and a half times what chance would hand you, not an order of magnitude
above it. The paired design makes the true null tighter than the independent
calculation, so the effect is probably real; the number to report is a
permutation one — within each review, shuffle which variant produced which of
its twelve answers, recompute the spread, repeat ten thousand times, and read
off where 14.67 falls. We did not run that,
and it is the first thing to add if you repeat this experiment.

[Almost fifteen points of accuracy, between two prompts that say the same
thing.]{.hl}

### Is that real, or is it 150 documents of noise?

The confidence intervals overlap, so the obvious next question is whether any of
this survives contact with statistics. The observed spread of 14.67 points is a
fact about these 150 documents; whether it generalises is the separate claim, and
the paired analysis below is how you interrogate it — it uses the item-level
disagreements directly instead of comparing two aggregate proportions.

```text
best  'label positive/negative'  90.00%
worst 'review first'             75.33%

  documents where they disagree            42
    best right, worst wrong                32
    worst right, best wrong                10
  McNemar exact test                    p = 0.0009
  Bonferroni over 66 pairs              p = 0.062
```

The intuition behind McNemar's test is a coin: if the two prompts were equally
good, each of the 42 disagreements would be equally likely to go either way,
and the exact test asks how surprising a 32–10 split is for a fair coin tossed
42 times. Bonferroni then multiplies that raw $p$ by the number of comparisons
you could have made — here 66.

The difference survives an uncorrected paired test — and *best against worst* is
the extreme of the $\binom{12}{2} = 66$ possible pairs, chosen after looking at
the data, so the uncorrected number is not the one to quote. Corrected for those
66 comparisons it lands at **p = 0.062**: suggestive, and not significant at the
5% level after correction, on 150 items. That is Bonferroni. Holm would need the
full ranking of all 66 p-values, and the largest accuracy gap is not guaranteed
to be the smallest paired p-value, so we do not quote a Holm figure we have not
computed.

The honest primary test is the omnibus one — Cochran's Q across all twelve
variants on the same 150 items — because that is the question actually being
asked: *does the prompt matter at all?* Run Q first, then Holm-corrected
pairwise McNemar for the pairs you want to name. We report the pair because it
is the one people quote, but treat the effect as a **spread**. The next
statistic measures that spread directly, avoids the multiple-comparison problem,
and does not involve accuracy at all:

```text
all 12 variants give the same answer on   104/150 = 69.3% of reviews
the prompt decides the answer on           46/150 = 30.7%

two variants disagree on: median 12.0% of reviews, max 28.7%
```

**On three reviews in ten, the answer changed across the twelve tested prompt
variants.** The review, the model, the temperature and the seed were all held
fixed, so the prompt is what moved — though "the prompt" here covers label
wording, role, ordering and politeness, not formatting alone. Note what that first number is and is not: twelve
variants *agreeing* does not mean the agreed answer is right, and this run does
not report accuracy on the unanimous 104 separately. Add that row when you
repeat the experiment — it is the difference between "the model has an opinion"
as a measurement and as a figure of speech, and the next subsection shows how
much rests on it.

### Is the prompt deciding, or is it moving a threshold?

Follow the arithmetic before you accept the framing, because it points somewhere
more useful. If the 104 unanimous reviews are all correct, then the mean score
of 82.06% — 123.1 of 150 — leaves **19.1 of the 46 contested reviews correct.
That is 41.5%, below the 50% floor of a balanced task.** The best variant gets
31 of the 46 and the worst gets 9.

Twelve prompts answering at random on hard items would sit at 50%. Sitting
*below* 50% on average, with the extremes at 67% and 20%, points to a different
picture: twelve prompts at twelve different **thresholds**, each systematically
leaning toward one label.

Hold that reading loosely, because it rests on the "all correct" assumption. If
just four of the 104 unanimous reviews were wrong, the contested 46 would be at
50.2%, not 41.5%. And a below-chance score on a subset *chosen because the
prompts disagree on it* can also come from reviews whose gold label is itself
debatable. The threshold story is the hypothesis to test, not the conclusion.

Which points at a fix the prompt-engineering framing hides.
@zhao2021calibrate showed that much of this sensitivity is *label bias* — the
model's prior over the answer tokens, shifted by surface features of the
prompt — and that estimating it on a content-free input (such as `N/A`) and
dividing it out substantially reduces the variance across prompt formats. The
fix needs the model's probabilities for the label tokens, not just the text it
returns; @sec-decoding shows how to read them. So the honest version of this section's result is:
**before calibration the prompt is worth 14.67 points.** How much of that
survives *after* is the experiment to run next, and reporting each variant's
$P(\text{predict positive})$ on a balanced set — which should be 50% and
almost certainly is not — is the one-column diagnostic that would have shown
this without any of the arithmetic above.

bands. The top band is the chapter's headline number in a different form: all
twelve variants give the same answer on 104 of the 150, and on the remaining 46
the choice of variant decides the answer. That is agreement, not accuracy. The bottom band is why the statistics work — a paired test looks
only at the 42 reviews where the two prompts differ, which is how it separates
scores whose confidence intervals overlap.
:::

### What that means for everything else you measure

Put this next to @sec-classification's result on the same model. There, writing
the *instruction* in English rather than Turkish — the single most repeated
piece of prompting folklore — was worth **+0.54 macro-F1**, with a 95% interval
running only to +2.25: not a demonstration that the effect is gone, but a
ceiling of just over two points on whatever remains. Here, changing the *bullet
formatting* is worth eight. The two numbers come from different tasks and
metrics — complaint detection scored by macro-F1 on 2,000 documents there,
balanced sentiment scored by accuracy on 150 here — so read the comparison as
one of orders of magnitude, not as a precise ratio.

Read the table again before concluding that language does not matter, though,
because it complicates the folklore rather than killing it. Changing the *label*
from `positive`/`negative` to `olumlu`/`olumsuz` cost **12 points** against the
`label positive/negative` variant — the largest single-variable change in this
experiment. (Against `baseline` the same two Turkish words cost only 1.33
points, so which reference you pick matters; the variants' full texts, which
this chapter does not print, are what would settle the cleaner comparison.)
Instruction language did almost nothing; label language did more than any
formatting change. "Does language matter?" is not one
question, and the two halves of it gave opposite answers on the same model.

[The variable everyone argues about was noise where they argue about it, and the
largest effect in the experiment was two words nobody thinks of as a
variable.]{.hl}

Three consequences, and the third is the one that changes how you work:

1. **A single-prompt model comparison is unreliable.** If the prompt spread on
   one model is 14.67 points, then "model A beat model B by 5 points" measured
   with one prompt each is a statement about the prompts. Compare models over a
   *set* of prompts and report the distribution, or accept that you have not
   compared the models.
2. **Your reported accuracy needs an error bar you have not been computing.**
   The sampling interval on 150 documents spans about 12 points end to end. The
   prompt spread, on the same data, is 14.67 — the same order of magnitude,
   which is the point: one of those error bars is computed and printed and the
   other is neither. Note also that they respond differently to more data. Add
   documents and the sampling interval keeps shrinking toward zero; the observed
   prompt spread shrinks only until the sampling noise inside it is gone, and
   then stays at the true prompt effect.
3. **Prompt changes need regression tests, not review.** No reviewer reading
   "moved the review above the instruction" would predict −4 points, because
   the change is semantically empty. Only a measurement catches it, which is
   what makes this a testing problem rather than a writing problem.

::: {.column-margin}
@sclar2024quantifying is the systematic version of this experiment across
tasks and models, and it finds the same thing at scale: spurious formatting
features move scores by amounts comparable to real model differences.
@lu2022fantastically found the same for the *order* of demonstrations, and their
result is the sharper one: permuting a *fixed* set of examples moved scores from
near state-of-the-art to near chance, the examples identical and only their
sequence changed. The `review first` variant above is the zero-shot shadow of
that effect; in a few-shot prompt the ordering degree of freedom can be larger
than the formatting one measured here, and you are almost certainly not measuring
it. The
literature has been clear about this for years; the practice has not caught
up, because the prompt still feels like a message rather than a component.
:::

### The patterns that lost

Two results in that table are worth naming because they contradict widely
taught advice.

**The role prefix came 11th of 12** (76.00%, against 79.33% for the same
prompt without it). *You are an experienced customer-feedback analyst* is the
most reproduced prompting pattern in circulation, and on this task it cost
three points.

**Politeness cost 2.67 points** (four reviews of 150). *Lütfen… Teşekkürler* is harmless-looking and
it is not free.

Neither result generalises — that is the point. They are two more variables
that a competent reader would call irrelevant and the model does not. The
lesson is not "never use a role prefix"; it is that [you cannot tell which
prompt is better by reading them]{.hl}, and the belief that you can is what
this whole section is arguing against.

## Making prompt work reviewable {#sec-prompting-eval}

If the prompt is a component and its effect is 14.67 points, it needs the
machinery any other component gets. Four pieces, in the order they pay off.

### 1. Pin down reproducibility first

Before measuring anything, find out whether your setup returns the same answer
twice. Thirty reviews, ten repeats each:

```text
setting                          identical output   documents that varied
temperature 0, fixed seed              100.0%              0 / 30
temperature 0, no seed                 100.0%              0 / 30
temperature 0.7, fixed seed            100.0%              0 / 30
temperature 0.7, no seed                 3.3%             29 / 30
```

Good news and a trap. **At temperature 0 this setup returned identical output on
all 30 documents across ten repeats, with or without a seed, and a fixed seed
did the same at temperature 0.7.** Read that as *no variation in 300 calls*
rather than as a proof of determinism: zero events in 30 items still leaves room
for a true variation rate of up to about 10%. Without either, 29 of 30 documents
gave a different answer across ten runs — so an evaluation at default settings
is measuring the sampler as much as the prompt.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
That table is a single local server answering one request at a time, and *that*
is the load-bearing condition — not that the server is local. What breaks
determinism is a lack of **batch invariance**: the reduction kernels behind matmul,
normalisation and attention take different code paths at different batch sizes,
so the same prompt in a batch of one and in a batch of seventeen can decode
differently even at temperature 0 [@he2025nondeterminism]. Hosted APIs batch
your request with strangers, which is why they are frequently non-deterministic
at temperature 0 — but a local server is not automatically safe either. Change
the batch size, the context length, the KV-cache reuse or the backend and the
same thing happens. Do not assume; run the ten-repeat check against the endpoint
*and the configuration* you will actually ship on, and if it is not
deterministic, your eval needs repeats and an interval rather than a single
number.
:::

### 2. Build a small evaluation set, and freeze it

Once you know the setup answers the same way twice, you need something to
answer *about*. Fifty to two hundred items, labelled by you, covering the
failure modes you have already seen. It does not need to be large — it needs
to be *fixed*, so that two prompt versions are comparable.

The discipline from @sec-classification applies unchanged: hold it out, look at
it as rarely as possible, and never tune a prompt against the same items you
report on.

A prompt tuned on its evaluation set is exactly as overfitted as a model tuned
on its test set, and far easier to do by accident — because iterating on a
prompt feels like writing rather than fitting.

### 3. Compare paired, not independently

This is the statistical point @sec-prompting-brittle turned on. Two prompts run
on the *same* items are a paired comparison, so use the pairing: count the
documents where they disagree, and test that count.

```text
prompt A right, B wrong     32
prompt B right, A wrong     10
                            --
McNemar exact            p = 0.0009
```

Comparing two accuracy figures with overlapping confidence intervals would
have called that inconclusive. The paired test calls it decisively, from the
same 150 documents, because it throws away the 108 items both prompts agree
on — which carry no information about the difference.

### 4. Version the template, not the string

Store the template with slots, in the repository, with a version. Log which
version produced each output. When something regresses, the question *which
prompt was this* has to have an answer, and "the one in the notebook" is not
one.

```python
PROMPTS = {
    "sentiment/v3": "...",     # bulleted, labels positive/negative
    "sentiment/v4": "...",     # + explicit null case
}
```

Two habits that fall out of it: the assembled prompt is a *build artefact* and
should not be edited by hand, and a prompt change ships with its evaluation
delta the way a code change ships with tests.

## Intuition checks {#sec-prompting-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. All six are questions this chapter settled
with a measurement rather than an argument.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Model A beat model B by 5 points on your eval. Which is better?

You do not know, because you have not separated the model from the prompt.
Measured on one model, one task and twelve semantically identical prompts, the
spread was **14.67 points** — three times the gap you are trying to interpret.

Run both models over a *set* of prompts and compare the distributions. If that
is too expensive, at least run each model on two or three prompts and report
the range. A single-prompt comparison is a statement about the prompts.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your reviewer says "moving the input above the instruction is a no-op." Are they right?

Semantically yes, empirically no: it cost **4.00 points** here (79.33% → 75.33%).

That is the whole argument for treating prompts as testable components. No
reviewer can predict that by reading, because there is nothing to read — the
change is meaning-preserving. The only thing that catches it is running the
evaluation, which makes prompt changes a testing problem rather than a writing
problem.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Does "You are an expert…" help?

On this task it came 11th of 12, at 76.00% against 79.33% for the same prompt
without it.

Do not over-read that either — it is one task and one model, and the point is
not that role prefixes are bad. The point is that the most-reproduced pattern
in prompting lost to its own baseline here, and nobody would have guessed the
sign. Measure it on your task; it takes one extra run.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your few-shot examples have wrong labels. How bad is that?

Less bad than you would think, which tells you something about what
demonstrations are for. @min2022rethinking randomised the labels in the
demonstrations and most of the benefit survived, because what the examples
mainly convey is the *format and the label space* rather than the mapping.

Practical readings: do not spend a week hand-curating examples before checking
whether examples help at all; and if your task's difficulty is in the mapping
rather than the format, expect demonstrations to underdeliver.

What does move the number is *which* examples you show — @liu2022makes found
that retrieving demonstrations semantically close to the input beats choosing
them at random, which turns example selection into a retrieval problem and
hands it to @sec-retrieval's machinery.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Is temperature 0 reproducible?

Locally, here, yes — 100% identical across ten repeats, with or without a
seed. On a hosted API, often not, because batching changes floating-point
reduction order and your request shares a batch with strangers.

Run the check rather than assuming: same prompt, same input, ten times,
against the endpoint you will ship on. If it varies, every number in your
evaluation needs repeats and an interval.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. When should a prompt stop being a prompt?

When you are maintaining a specification rather than writing a request. The
signals: the prompt has a version history, its output is parsed by code, a
change to it can break a downstream consumer, and you cannot safely edit it
without running something.

At that point it is a component of your system and belongs under the same
discipline as the rest of your code — repository, version, contract,
regression test. @sec-decoding is where the output contract gets *enforced*
rather than requested.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-prompting-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's own
measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the mechanism

**Q: What actually happens when you put examples in a prompt?**

Nothing is learned in the training sense — no weight changes and nothing
survives the call. The examples narrow which task the model performs, which is
why it is better described as task inference than as learning. Then deliver
the result that shows you have read past the tutorial: @min2022rethinking
randomised the demonstration labels and most of the benefit survived, so what
examples largely convey is the format and label space rather than the mapping.

**Q: Why did prompting stop feeling like a trick?**

Because instruction tuning happened. A base model continues text, so early
prompting meant constructing a prefix whose natural continuation was the
answer. Instruction tuning, followed by preference training
(@sec-post-training), trained models to treat an instruction as an instruction. Candidates who cannot separate "the model got
bigger" from "the model got trained to follow instructions" have not thought
about where the capability came from.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: Two prompts, which is better?**

Run both on the same frozen evaluation set and use a **paired** test — count
the items where they disagree and test that count, not the two accuracies.
Measured here, two prompts with overlapping confidence intervals were
separated at $p = 0.0009$ by McNemar, because the pairing discards the items
on which both gave the same answer, right or wrong.

If the answer is "I read them and the second is clearer", the candidate has
not measured a prompt.

**Q: How much of your reported accuracy is the prompt?**

The honest answer is that most teams do not know, and the measurement is a
morning's work: write several semantically identical prompts and run all of
them. Here twelve of them spanned **14.67 points**, and all twelve agreed on
only **69.3%** of items — so on three items in ten the choice of prompt variant decided
the output. That number is an error bar that almost nobody reports, and here
it was larger than the sampling interval.

**Q: How do you stop prompt changes from breaking production?**

Treat the prompt as a versioned component: template in the repository, version
logged with every output, a frozen evaluation set, and a delta reported with
every change. Then say why review is not enough — a semantically empty edit
cost 4 points here and no reviewer would have predicted it.

**Q: Your evaluation results changed and nothing was deployed. What happened?**

Check reproducibility before anything else. Same prompt, same input, ten
repeats. Locally, temperature 0 showed no variation in 300 calls here; without a seed
at temperature 0.7, 29 of 30 items varied. And hosted endpoints are often
non-deterministic even at temperature 0, because batching changes
floating-point reduction order — so the answer may be that nothing happened
and your eval never had an interval on it.

## The 2026 toolbox {#sec-prompting-tools}

Everything in this chapter ran on one laptop with the versions below.

| library | version used | what it is for here |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `ollama` | 0.24.0 | serving `qwen3.5:9b` for every measurement in this chapter |
| Python stdlib | 3.14.5 | the experiment is a `for` loop over prompts and a paired test; it needed no framework |

: The stack these numbers came from {tbl-colwidths="[24,16,60]"}

Worth knowing about, not used above:

| library | current version | when you would reach for it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `promptfoo` | 0.122.0 (npm) | prompt A/B testing and regression suites as a config file — the tooling version of @sec-prompting-eval, and the fastest way to stop doing this in notebooks |
| `dspy` | 3.3.1 | stops you writing prompt strings at all: declare the signature, let it compile the prompt against a metric. The right answer once you accept that hand-tuning a brittle artefact is a poor use of a week |
| `instructor` / `pydantic` | 1.15.4 / 2.13.4 | the output contract of @sec-prompting-spec as a Python type, validated on arrival |
| `guidance` | 0.3.1 | constrains generation to a template or grammar — @sec-decoding's machinery, applied at the prompt layer |
| `jinja2` | 3.1.6 | prompt templates with slots, versioned as files. Unglamorous, and it solves the "which prompt produced this" problem outright |
| `langsmith` | 0.11.1 | tracing and dataset management when the pipeline outgrows a spreadsheet |
| `pytest` | 9.1.1 | the point being that a prompt regression suite is just tests, and needs no LLM-specific framework to start |

: The wider ecosystem, versions as of writing {tbl-colwidths="[22,16,62]"}

::: {.column-margin}
`dspy` deserves the second look its position does not give it. Its premise is
exactly this chapter's finding: if prompt wording moves the score by amounts
you cannot predict, then hand-writing prompts is optimisation by guesswork,
and a compiler with a metric will beat you. The cost is that your prompts stop
being readable artefacts, which is a real trade rather than a free win.
:::

## Lab: turn a prompt into a component {#sec-prompting-lab}

Take a task you actually do — one where you have been iterating on a prompt by
feel. The lab converts it into something with a version and an error bar.

### Step 1 — freeze two sets, not one

Label a **development** set you will iterate on and a **final** set you will
open once, at the end. Fifty each is a workable minimum. Include the failures
you already know about; that is what makes them useful rather than decorative.
Split before you look at anything, write both to files, and stop editing them.

Everything from step 2 to step 5 runs on the development set. Every number you
report on the development set is a number you selected for, and reporting it as
your system's accuracy is the mistake this whole chapter is about — you would
be quoting a score tuned on the set that produced it.

### Step 2 — measure reproducibility before anything else

Same prompt, same input, ten repeats, against the endpoint you will ship on.
If the answers vary, every number below needs repeats and an interval, and you
need to know that now rather than after a confusing week.

### Step 3 — write six prompts that mean the same thing

Not six *better* prompts — six that a colleague would call identical. Vary
formatting, label surface form, delimiters, the position of the input, a role
prefix. Run all six.

The spread you get is your prompt's error bar. Write it down; it is the number
that tells you how seriously to take every comparison you have made so far.

### Step 4 — pick the winner with a paired test

Best against worst on the development set, McNemar on the disagreements. Report
the number of items where they differ, not just the two accuracies — and if you
picked the pair after seeing all six, correct for the
$\binom{6}{2} = 15$ comparisons you could have made.

### Step 5 — rewrite the winner as a specification

Output contract, explicit failure value, constraints near the end. Re-run on
the development set. Report whether the score moved and whether the *parse*
failures went to zero, which is usually the larger win.

### Step 6 — open the final set, once

Run the prompt you chose on the set you have not touched, and report *that*
number as your system's accuracy with an interval on it. Expect it to be lower
than the development figure; the gap is what your iteration cost you in
optimism, and it is worth knowing. If you go back and change the prompt after
seeing it, you have spent the set and need a new one.

### Step 7 — put it under version control and break it on purpose

Template with slots in a file, version string logged with each output. Then
make a semantically empty edit — reorder two sentences — and run the
evaluation. If the number moves, you have just demonstrated to yourself why
this is a testing problem.

### What to hand in

The six-prompt spread, the paired test for your winner, the before-and-after
for the specification rewrite, and one paragraph on what your prompt's error
bar means for the model comparison you most recently believed.

## Exercises {#sec-prompting-exercises}

1. **Your own brittleness number.** Six semantically identical prompts, one
   task, one model. Report the spread and the fraction of items where all six
   agree. Compare the spread against the difference between the two models you
   are choosing between.

2. **Paired versus unpaired.** Take two prompts whose confidence intervals
   overlap. Compute an unpaired comparison and a McNemar test on the same
   data. Report both, and say which you would put in a report and why.

3. **The $k$-shot curve this chapter does not have.** Run your task at
   $k \in \{0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\}$ demonstrations, twice: once with the gold
   labels and once with the labels shuffled. Plot both curves. If they rise
   together, the demonstrations are conveying *format*; if the gold curve pulls
   away, they are conveying the *mapping* — which is @min2022rethinking against
   @pan2023incontext on your own data. Then permute a fixed set of four
   demonstrations eight ways at fixed $k$ and report that spread too; per
   @lu2022fantastically it may be the larger of the two effects.

4. **The role prefix, on your task.** Run the same prompt with and without
   *You are an expert…*. Predict the sign before you run it. Report both.

5. **Reproducibility on your endpoint.** Ten repeats at temperature 0 against a
   hosted API and against a local model. If they differ, explain the mechanism
   to a colleague in two sentences.

6. **Request to specification.** Take a prompt written as a request, rewrite it
   as a contract with an explicit failure value, and count parse failures
   before and after. Then find an input where the failure value is the correct
   answer and check that the model actually returns it.

7. **The regression you cannot see.** Make a meaning-preserving edit to a
   production prompt — reorder sentences, change bullets to prose. Run your
   evaluation. If nothing moved, try three more edits before concluding your
   task is robust.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-prompting-deeper}

One exercise beats any reading here: write your prompt twice, changing only
formatting, and score both on the same hundred items. Whatever you read next
will land differently once you have seen your own spread.

## What to remember {#sec-prompting-summary}

- **In-context learning updates no parameters.** Nothing is fitted and nothing
  survives the call, which is why *task inference* describes the common case
  better than *learning* — with the caveat below that task learning is real and
  grows with scale. @min2022rethinking randomised the labels in
  the demonstrations and most of the benefit remained, which says examples
  mainly convey format and label space rather than the mapping.

- **The prompt is part of the model.** Twelve prompts that a competent reader
  would call the same instruction spanned **14.67 accuracy points** on one
  model and one task — 75.33% to 90.00%. That is not a writing difference; it
  is a component with an effect size.

- **On 30.7% of items, the answer changed across the twelve variants.** All
  twelve agreed on only 69.3% of the reviews; two variants disagreed on a
  median of 12% and as much as 28.7%. Your model has a stable answer on most
  items and the prompt moves the rest.

- **The spread is 14.67 points on these items, and the paired analysis is how
  you interrogate it.** Best against worst: overlapping confidence intervals, 42
  disagreements, McNemar **$p = 0.0009$** — but that pair was chosen after
  seeing the data, so the number to quote is the one corrected for all 66 pairs,
  **$p = 0.062$**. Suggestive; not significant at the 5% level after correction.
  The pairing uses information the unpaired comparison throws away, and the
  correction says how much of the result to believe.

- **Which means a single-prompt model comparison is unreliable.** If the prompt
  spread is 14.67 points, "model A beat model B by 5" measured with one
  prompt each is a statement about prompts. Compare over a set of prompts and
  report the distribution.

- **The folklore variable was noise and the ignored one was the effect.**
  @sec-classification measured English-versus-Turkish instructions at
  **+0.54, $p = 0.54$** on this same model. Bullet formatting, here, was
  worth eight points. The role prefix — the most reproduced pattern in
  circulation — came 11th of 12 and cost 3.33 points against its own baseline.

- **You cannot tell which prompt is better by reading them.** That is the whole
  case for treating prompt changes as a testing problem: a semantically empty
  edit cost 4.00 points, and no reviewer would have predicted the sign.

- **Check reproducibility before you measure anything.** Locally, temperature 0
  gave identical output on every repeat with or without a seed, and so did a
  fixed seed at temperature 0.7 — but with neither, 29 of 30 items varied
  across ten runs. Hosted APIs are frequently non-deterministic even at
  temperature 0, because batching changes floating-point reduction order. Run
  the ten-repeat check on the endpoint you will ship on.

- **Write prompts as specifications.** Name the output contract, name the
  failure value, and put constraints where they bind. Then validate the
  contract — a schema you do not check is a comment, and
  @sec-sequence-labeling-llm already showed that a schema guarantees shape and
  never truth.
